{{short description|Statistical test for dose-response trends}}

'''Tukey's trend test''' (or the '''Tukey-Ciminera-Heyse trend test''') is a [[non-parametric statistics|non-parametric]] or semi-parametric [[statistical hypothesis test]] used to detect a [[dose–response relationship]] between a discrete independent variable (such as dosage level) and a continuous dependent variable.

First proposed by [[John Tukey]], Joseph Ciminera, and John Heyse in 1985, the test was developed to address the limitations of [[simple linear regression]] when the exact functional form of the dose-response curve is unknown.<ref name="Tukey1985">{{Cite journal |last=Tukey |first=J. W. |last2=Ciminera |first2=J. L. |last3=Heyse |first3=J. F. |date=March 1985 |title=Testing the statistical certainty of a response to increasing doses of a drug |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4005384 |journal=Biometrics |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=295–301 |issn=0006-341X |pmid=4005384}}</ref> It is frequently applied in [[toxicology]] and [[pharmacology]] to determine if increasing exposure to a substance correlates with a monotonic increase or decrease in a biological response.

==Background==
In clinical and laboratory experiments, researchers often test a [[control group]] alongside several increasing dose levels (e.g., control, low, medium, and high). While a [[one-way ANOVA]] can identify  differences between dose groups, it does not account for the ordered nature of the doses. On the other hand, standard linear regression assumes a strictly linear relationship, which may fail to detect trends that are concave, convex, or [[step function]]s.

Tukey's trend test provides a robust alternative by using a "maximum-type" test statistic. It simultaneously considers multiple possible "shapes" of the trend, reducing the risk of a [[Type II error]] when the true dose-response shape is non-linear.<ref name="Bretz2002">{{Cite journal |last=Bretz |first=Frank |last2=Hothorn |first2=Ludwig A. |date=2002-11-30 |title=Detecting dose-response using contrasts: asymptotic power and sample size determination for binomial data |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12407675 |journal=Statistics in Medicine |volume=21 |issue=22 |pages=3325–3335 |doi=10.1002/sim.1324 |issn=0277-6715 |pmid=12407675}}</ref>

==Methodology==
The test typically evaluates a null hypothesis (<math>H_0</math>) of no trend against an alternative hypothesis (<math>H_A</math>) of a monotonic trend.

===Scoring shapes===
The original Tukey trend test employs three different sets of scores (<math>x</math>) to represent potential dose-response shapes:
# Arithmetic: assumes equal increments between doses (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3).
# Ordinal: ranks the doses regardless of their physical value (e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4)
# Logarithmic: assumes the effect is proportional to the logarithm of the dose (e.g., <math>0, \ln(d_{1}+1), \ln(d_{2}+1), \dots</math>

===Test statistic and correlation===
Testing for a trend is treated as a regression problem. For each set of scores, a [[t-statistic]] is calculated, based on the [[Pearson correlation coefficient]] (<math>r</math>) between the response (<math>Y</math>) and the assigned dose scores (<math>x</math>). For each score, its corresponding t-statistic is defined as:
:<math>t=\frac{r\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}</math>
where <math>n</math> is the total number of observations. The t-statistics are denoted <math>t_\text{arith}</math>, <math>t_\text{ord}</math>, and <math>t_\log</math> respectively, and quantify the level of "statistical certainty" that the slope of the relationship is non-zero. The final test statistic is formed as the maximum of these individual statistics:
:<math>T_\max = \max\left(t_\text{arith}, t_\text{ord}, t_\log\right)</math>

Because <math>T_\max</math> is the maximum of several correlated statistics, it does not follow a standard [[Student's t-distribution]]. Instead, the corresponding [[p-value]] must be adjusted, either via a [[multivariate t-distribution]] or through [[permutation test|permutation]] methods.<ref name="Schaarschmidt2022">{{Cite journal |last=Schaarschmidt |first=Frank |last2=Ritz |first2=Christian |last3=Hothorn |first3=Ludwig A. |date=June 2022 |title=The Tukey trend test: Multiplicity adjustment using multiple marginal models |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33559878 |journal=Biometrics |volume=78 |issue=2 |pages=789–797 |doi=10.1111/biom.13442 |issn=1541-0420 |pmid=33559878}}</ref>

==Significance and regulatory context==
It is often cited as a precursor to the [[Multiple Comparison Procedures and Modeling]] (MCP-MOD) approach.<ref name="Bretz2005">{{cite journal |last1=Bretz |first1=F. |last2=Pinheiro |first2=J. C. |last3=Branson |first3=M. |year=2005 |title=Combining multiple comparisons and modeling techniques in dose-response studies |journal=[[Biometrics (journal)|Biometrics]] |volume=61 |issue=3 |pages=738–748 |doi=10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00344.x}}</ref> While Tukey's 1985 test used a fixed set of three contrasts, MCP-MOD generalizes this to any number of candidate parametric models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pinheiro |first1=Jose |last2=Bornkamp |first2=Björn|last3=Glimm |first3=Ekkehard|last4=Bretz|first4=Franz |title= Model-based dose finding under model uncertainty using general parametric models|journal=Stat Med|date=May 2014| volume=33|issue=10| pages=1646–61| url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24302486/|doi=10.1002/sim.6052| PMID=24302486|arxiv=1305.0889}}</ref>

In 2014, the [[European Medicines Agency]] (EMA) issued a positive qualification opinion on MCP-MOD as an efficient methodology for [[Phases of clinical research|Phase II]] dose-finding studies.<ref>{{cite web |title=Qualification opinion of MCP-Mod as an efficient statistical methodology |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/regulatory-procedural-guideline/qualification-opinion-mcp-mod-efficient-statistical-methodology-model-based-design-and-analysis-phase-ii-dose-finding-studies-under-model-uncertainty_en.pdf |publisher=European Medicines Agency |date=2014 |access-date=11 January 2026}}</ref> The [[Food and Drug Administration]] gave a similar endorsement in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |last=Food and Drug Administration |title=U.S. FDA Qualification of The MCP-Mod Procedure |url=https://www.fda.gov/media/99313/download |website=FDA.gov |publisher=U.S. Department of Health and Human Services |date=July 2016 |access-date=January 11, 2026 |format=PDF}}</ref>

==Comparison to other tests==
Unlike the [[Jonckheere's trend test]], which is fully non-parametric and based on ranks, Tukey's trend test is more closely related to regression-based approaches.
